extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical geometry; mathematicians and historians studying Archimedes' On the Sphere and Cylinder
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of propositions and constructions from Archimedes' On the Sphere and Cylinder (Book I and beginning of Book II), giving exact relations between surfaces and volumes of spheres, cylinders, cones, and solids of revolution, and constructive problems for equal-volume/area solids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 27 — Volume bound for inscribed solid
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure inscribed in the sphere as before is less than four times the cone whose base is equal to a great circle of the sphere and whose height is equal to the radius of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: by Prop. 26 the volume equals a cone whose base equals the surface of the solid and whose height is p (perpendicular from center O on any side). Let R be that cone and S be cone with base equal to great circle and height equal to radius. Since surface of inscribed solid < 4 × great circle [Prop. 25] and p < radius, base(R) < 4 × base(S) and height(R) < height(S), hence vol(R) < 4 × vol(S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 28 — Circumscribed revolution figure larger than sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: A figure obtained by revolving a regular polygon (with number of sides multiple of four) circumscribed about a great circle is greater (has greater surface) than the sphere itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Each portion of surface described by polygon side (conical surface) entirely includes the corresponding rotated circular segment; since both are concave same way and the polygonal-generated surface includes the circular-generated one, the circumscribed figure's surface > sphere's surface (add over all sides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 29 — Surface of circumscribed figure equals a circle (formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the figure circumscribed to a sphere as in Prop. 28 the surface is equal to a circle the square on whose radius is equal to AB(BB' + CC' + ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: circumscribed figure is inscribed in a larger sphere; apply Prop. 24 (earlier) which gives representation of surface as circle with radius squared equal to that rectangle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 30 — Surface of circumscribed figure > 4 × great circle
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of a figure circumscribed about a sphere (as before) is greater than four times the great circle of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Prop. 29 compute radius of circle equal to surface and show it exceeds diameter of great circle (using relations between polygon side lengths and tangency), hence surface > 4 × great circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 31 — Volume of circumscribed solid equals cone with base equal to its surface and height = radius
rubrics_metrics.description: The solid of revolution circumscribed as before about a sphere is equal to a cone whose base is equal to the surface of the solid and whose height is equal to the radius of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the circumscribed solid is inscribed in a larger sphere and perpendicular on any side of revolving polygon equals radius of inner sphere, so identical with Prop. 26's statement for inscribed solids. (Therefore the volume equals that cone.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary to Prop. 31 — Volume bound for circumscribed solid
rubrics_metrics.description: The solid circumscribed about the smaller sphere is greater than four times the cone whose base is a great circle of the sphere and whose height is equal to the radius of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Prop. 30 (surface of circumscribed solid > 4×great circle) and Lemma: cone with base = surface and height = radius is > 4×cone with same height and base = great circle; by Prop. 31 the solid's volume equals that cone, so conclusion follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 32 (1) — Surface ratio of circumscribed to inscribed solids
rubrics_metrics.description: If similar regular polygons of 4n sides are inscribed and circumscribed about a great circle and revolved to form inscribed and circumscribed solids, then the surfaces of the circumscribed and inscribed figures are to one another in the duplicate ratio of their sides (i.e. ratio of squares of corresponding side lengths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive formulas for circle-radii representing surfaces: (radius_R)^2 = AB(BB' + CC' + ...) and (radius_S)^2 = ab(bb' + cc' + ...). Since polygons are similar the rectangles are similar and scale as AB^2 : ab^2, hence surfaces scale as AB^2:ab^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 32 (2) — Volume ratio of circumscribed to inscribed solids
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the same setup the volumes of the circumscribed and inscribed figures are in the triplicate ratio of their sides (i.e. ratio of cubes of corresponding side lengths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct cones equal to the solids (by Propositions 31 and 26): bases scale as AB^2:ab^2 and heights scale as AB:ab (since similar polygons give proportional perpendiculars), so volumes (base×height) scale as AB^3:ab^3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 33 — Surface of sphere equals 4×greatest circle
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of any sphere is equal to four times the greatest circle in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by exhaustion/contradiction: assume 4×great circle is either less or greater than sphere's surface; inscribe and circumscribe similar regular polygons with 4n sides so that ratio of their sides approximates desired bounds and use Prop. 32 plus bounds on inscribed/circumscribed surfaces (Props. 23,25,28,30) to reach contradiction; hence equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 34 — Volume of sphere equals 4×cone (base = great circle, height = radius)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any sphere is equal (in volume) to four times the cone which has its base equal to the greatest circle in the sphere and its height equal to the radius of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using inscribed and circumscribed solids and their volume scalings (Prop. 32) and prior volume bounds (Props. 27,31) to show sphere cannot be larger or smaller than 4×cone, hence equal. Corollary: cylinder with base = great circle and height = diameter equals 3×sphere (surface relations also follow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary to Prop. 34 — Cylinder/sphere relations
rubrics_metrics.description: A cylinder whose base is the greatest circle in a sphere and whose height is equal to the diameter of the sphere is 3 of the sphere, and its surface together with its bases is 3/2 (?) of the surface of the sphere (text states cylinder is 3 of the sphere; surface with bases equals 3×great circle etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses relation: cylinder = 3×(cone with same base and height) (Euclid xi.10) and sphere = 4×that cone (Prop. 34), so cylinder = 3×sphere (text phrasing echoes classic Archimedean ratio relations; see surrounding argument for exact multiplicative factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 35 — Surface of inscribed solid in sphere segment equals a circle (formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polygon is inscribed in a segment of a circle and revolved about the diameter to generate an inscribed solid in a segment of a sphere, then the surface of the inscribed solid equals a circle whose square on radius equals the rectangle AB(BB' + CC' + ... + KK' + ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute surface as sum of cone/frustum surfaces generated by each side; by Prop. 14 and subsequent formulae the total surface equals a circle with radius given by the square-root of that rectangle (additive decomposition of cone/frustum contributions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 36 — Surface of inscribed figure < surface of spherical segment
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of the figure inscribed as before in the segment of a sphere is less than that of the segment of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the circular base is a common boundary and the spherical segment includes the inscribed solid while both are concave in same direction; Assumptions 4 used (inclusion implies larger surface).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 37 — Upper bound for inscribed-solid surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of the solid figure inscribed in the segment of the sphere by revolution of the polygon is less than a circle with radius equal to AL (a chord/endpoint distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express surface as circle with radius sqrt(AB(BB'+...)), show that rectangle equals A B · AM (Prop. 22) and that is less than AL^2, hence surface < circle of radius AL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 38 — Inscribed solid + cone equals a cone (volume identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The solid described (inscribed) in a segment of a sphere together with the cone whose base is the base of the segment and apex at the sphere's centre is equal to a cone whose base is equal to the surface of the inscribed solid and whose height is equal to the perpendicular from the centre to any side of the polygon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose the inscribed solid into parts generated by triangles; each such part equals a cone with base equal to the corresponding frustum surface and height p; adding gives the stated cone equality. Uses Props. 18 and 20 for rhombi/cone correspondences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary to Prop. 38 — Cone comparison bound
rubrics_metrics.description: The cone whose base is a circle of radius AL and whose height equals the sphere radius is greater than the sum of the inscribed solid and the cone OLL'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine Prop. 38 with Prop. 37 (surface bound) and inequality p < OA to compare heights and bases; hence inequality between cones follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 39 — Circumscribed solid about a sector > spherical segment
rubrics_metrics.description: A solid formed by revolving a polygon circumscribed about a sector of a great circle (less than a semicircle) is greater in surface than the spherical segment corresponding to that sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct tangents to inner segment and compare revolutions: the solid generated by revolution of tangents has larger surface than the segment (Assumptions, 4); since polygonal sides exceed tangent lengths, their revolution surface is even larger, so circumscribed figure surface > segment surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 39 Corollary — Surface formula for circumscribed sector-figure
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of the figure described about the sector is equal to a circle whose square on radius equals AB(BB' + CC' + ... + KR' + LL').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the circumscribed figure is inscribed in an outer sphere; apply same technique as Prop. 35/29 to represent surface as circle with radius derived from sum of rectangular contributions from sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 40 — Lower bound for circumscribed-sector surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of the figure circumscribed to the sector is greater than a circle whose radius equals al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Prop. 39 Corollary, express surface radius as sqrt(AB(BB'+...)) and show rectangle equals A'B·AM which exceeds am·a'd etc.; deduce the surface > circle radius al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 40 Corollaries (1 & 2) — Volume equalities and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Cor.1: Volume of circumscribed figure + cone with apex O and base circle on LL' equals the volume of a cone with base equal to surface of circumscribed figure and height ON. Cor.2: That volume is greater than cone whose base radius = al and height = radius Oa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cor.1: circumscribed figure is inscribed in outer sphere, thus apply Prop. 38 proof. Cor.2: combine Prop. 40 (surface > circle radius al) and equality of heights ON=Oa to compare volumes of cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 41 — Ratios for sector inscribed vs circumscribed solids
rubrics_metrics.description: For a sector (less than semicircle) with inscribed and circumscribed similar polygons (2n equal sides) revolved about bisector: (1) surfaces of outer and inner solids are in ratio AB^2 : ab^2; (2) their volumes together with corresponding cones with apex O are as AB^3 : ab^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use previous corollaries giving surfaces as circles with radii dependent on AB(BB'+...), and Prop. 38/40 corollaries for cone-volume identifications; similarity of polygons yields proportionality of rectangles and heights, giving duplicate and triplicate ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 42 — Surface of spherical segment equals circle radius al
rubrics_metrics.description: If lal' is a segment of a sphere (less than a hemisphere) and Oa the radius perpendicular to the base, then the surface of the segment equals a circle whose radius equals al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using circumscribed/inscribed polygon solids (Props. 39–41) and the inequalities of their surfaces to squeeze the segment surface between equal circles; neither larger nor smaller possible, hence equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 43 — Segment greater than a hemisphere still has same surface formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the segment of the sphere is greater than a hemisphere, its surface is still equal to a circle whose radius equals al (difference-of-spheres argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose full sphere into two segments; use Prop. 42 for the complementary segment and Prop. 33 for whole sphere; subtract surfaces (circles) to show the given segment's surface corresponds to radius al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 44 — Volume of sector equals cone with base = surface of segment and height = radius
rubrics_metrics.description: The volume of any sector of a sphere equals a cone whose base equals the surface of the spherical segment included in the sector, and whose height equals the radius of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction via approximation by inscribed/circumscribed polygonal solids and use of previous results (Props. 38, 40, 42, 43) to squeeze the sector volume to equality with that cone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II, Proposition 1 (Problem) — Construct sphere equal to given cone or cylinder
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a cone or cylinder V, construct a sphere equal in volume to V by building a cylinder equal to 3V whose height equals diameter of its base, then the sphere whose diameter equals that height is equal to V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthesis: find two mean proportionals between AB and OD (dimensions of an appropriate cylinder) to construct a cylinder with height equal to diameter of its base and equal volume; then the sphere with that diameter equals the given solid. Detailed proportional algebra and mean-proportionals construction provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II, Proposition 2 — Volume of spherical segment expressed as cone (with explicit height ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: If BAB' is a segment of a sphere with BB' diameter of base and AA' diameter bisecting BB' in M, then the volume of the segment equals that of a cone whose base is the same as the segment's base and whose height is h, where h:AM = OA^2 + A'M : A'M (explicit proportional relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct points H and H' along OA and OA' so that MH (and MH') equal the computed heights; show sector decomposition into cones/rhombi and use proportional relations and equality of cones to equate segment to cone HBB'. Alternative proof via considering cone equal to whole sphere and decomposing also provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II, Proposition 8 (Problem) — Cut sphere to obtain segments with given surface ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: To cut a given sphere by a plane so that the surfaces of the resulting segments have a prescribed ratio: using Archimedes' relation that segment surfaces equal circles of radii AB and A'B, choose M on diameter AA' so that AM:MA' equals that ratio (via dividing AD appropriately) and erect the plane through M perpendicular to AA'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because segment surfaces correspond to circles whose radii correspond to distances from bisecting radius, one reduces the problem to dividing AA' proportionally; constructive synthesis explains how to choose M using mean proportionals and the previous proportional identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II, Proposition 4 (Problem) — Cut sphere so that segment volumes have given ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: To cut a sphere by a plane so that the volumes of the segments are in a given ratio: reduce to determining points H, H' on OA and OA' so that cones HBB' and H'BB' (equal to segments) have altitudes in the given ratio; use proportional equations and elimination to locate M on AA'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed analytic elimination of auxiliary heights H, H' is provided: express A'H':H'M and HH':H'A' via OA, AM, and constructed D,E points; reduce to dividing a given segment AD at M with prescribed ratio relations; synthesis gives final construction and choice of M.
